# A. Rational Series

## How to find it

Compute `Q` inverse to precision `n`, then multiply by `P` and truncate.

## Correctness

Multiplying the output by `Q` gives `P` modulo `x^n` by the inverse invariant, which uniquely determines the quotient prefix.

## Complexity

`O(M(n))` time and `O(n)` storage.

This requires `Q[0]` to be nonzero. Truncation is essential: coefficients of
`P` or the inverse at degree at least `n` cannot affect the requested prefix.

# B. Connected Series

## How to find it

The assembly product becomes an additive connected-component series under formal logarithm.

## Correctness

The requested encoding defines the connected series as the unique zero-constant series whose exponential is `A`; formal log is its inverse.

## Complexity

`O(M(n))` time and `O(n)` storage.

Check the exact generating-function convention in the statement. The
constant term must be one before taking the normalized logarithm, and the
answer's constant term is zero.

# C. Archive Evaluation

## How to find it

Use one product tree; repeated keys need no special case because evaluation, unlike interpolation, permits repeated leaves.

## Correctness

Each leaf still receives the polynomial modulo `x-X_i`, so duplicates independently obtain the same correct value.

## Complexity

`O(M(n+q) log q)` time.

Repeated evaluation keys are allowed because no denominator is formed. Keep
them as separate leaves so output order and multiplicity are preserved.

# D. Recover Polynomial

## How to find it

Input order is irrelevant: pair each ordinate with its own leaf and use the product-tree Lagrange construction.

## Correctness

At `X_i`, every other basis term contains `X_i-X_i`, while its own term evaluates to one.

## Complexity

`O(M(n) log n)` time.

Unlike evaluation, interpolation requires distinct keys: otherwise
`M'(X_i)=0` can occur and the data need not identify a unique degree-bounded
polynomial. Shuffling the input pairs must not change the reconstructed answer.

# E. OR Convolution

## How to find it

Use subset zeta transform: a transformed coordinate sums all submasks.

## Correctness

Multiplying two zeta sums counts exactly pairs whose OR is a submask; Möbius subtraction isolates pairs with OR equal to each mask.

## Complexity

`O(k 2^k)` time and `O(2^k)` storage.

The forward loop adds each value into supersets; the inverse performs the same
traversal with subtraction. Reversing the subset relation silently produces
AND rather than OR convolution.

# F. Disjoint Cover Counts

## How to find it

This is subset convolution under a story name; use ranked zeta transforms.

## Correctness

The rank filter and Möbius inversion leave precisely ordered disjoint pairs whose union is the output mask.

## Complexity

`O(k squared 2^k)` time and `O(k 2^k)` storage.

The empty mask participates and must occupy rank zero. Ordered pairs are
counted because `F` supplies the first set and `G` the second; do not divide by
two even when the two arrays happen to be equal.

# Final verification

For A and B, substitute the result into the defining FPS identity. For C and
D, use Horner and direct Lagrange interpolation. For E and F, enumerate all
mask pairs. Run these independent oracles on every dimension small enough for
exhaustion, including all-zero data and singleton precision. The transform is
an optimization of the defining sum; that sum remains the clearest oracle.
